# Pharmacogenomics Report: Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma (LUSC)

**Sample summary:** Four somatic variants identified post-QC and germline filtering, all at similar variant allele frequencies (VAF ~35%), suggesting a clonal origin. Variants affect *PIK3CA*, *CDKN2A*, *TP53*, and *NFE2L2*.

---

## Overview

This tumour harbours four recurrently mutated genes in lung squamous cell carcinoma: a gain-of-function *PIK3CA* hotspot mutation (p.E545K), a loss-of-function *CDKN2A* truncation (p.R80*), a *TP53* hotspot missense (p.R248Q), and an *NFE2L2* activating missense (p.R34G). Together these represent a genomic profile typical of LUSC [PMID 22960745].

**Headline:** There is **no approved targeted therapy** for this specific variant combination in LUSC as a standard-of-care indication. *PIK3CA* p.E545K is the most actionable variant and provides a rationale for PI3K pathway inhibition, but no PI3Kα inhibitor is currently approved for LUSC. Alpelisib (BYL719) is approved in *PIK3CA*-mutant hormone receptor-positive breast cancer and is under investigation in other solid tumours. Immunotherapy (PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors) remains the backbone of systemic treatment for LUSC and is not addressed in this pharmacogenomics report, which focuses on targeted agents.

---

## A. Established Clinical Evidence

### A1. *PIK3CA* p.E545K — PI3Kα inhibition

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Drug** | Alpelisib (BYL719) |
| **Approval** | FDA-approved for *PIK3CA*-mutant HR+/HER2− advanced breast cancer (SOLAR-1 trial) [PMID 31091374] |
| **Evidence level in LUSC** | **Level 3B** (approved in a different tumour type; no LUSC-specific approval) |
| **Variant** | p.E545K is a well-characterised helical-domain activating hotspot in *PIK3CA*, functionally equivalent to p.E542K; both are included in the SOLAR-1 companion diagnostic [PMID 31091374] |

**Rationale:** *PIK3CA* p.E545K activates the PI3K–AKT–mTOR axis by disrupting an inhibitory interaction between the helical domain and the regulatory subunit p85 [PMID 15016963]. This is one of the most common *PIK3CA* mutations in LUSC (~5–7% of cases) [PMID 22960745]. Alpelisib selectively inhibits PI3Kα and demonstrated progression-free survival benefit in breast cancer harbouring this class of mutation [PMID 31091374]. A basket trial (MATCH sub-protocol Z1F) evaluated alpelisib in *PIK3CA*-mutant non-breast solid tumours including lung; preliminary results showed modest single-agent activity (objective response rate ~5%), suggesting limited efficacy as monotherapy in LUSC [PMID 35417260]. Combination strategies (e.g., with mTOR inhibitors or chemotherapy) are under investigation.

**No other PI3K pathway inhibitor is currently approved for LUSC.** Idelalisib (PI3Kδ) and copanlisib (pan-PI3K) are approved only in haematological malignancies [PMID 24631838, PMID 28985528].

---

### A2. *TP53* p.R248Q — No approved targeted therapy in LUSC

*TP53* mutations are present in ~80% of LUSC [PMID 22960745]. p.R248Q is a dominant-negative gain-of-function hotspot that abrogates DNA-contact with target sequences and confers oncogenic properties [PMID 1565143]. **No TP53-directed agent is currently approved for any solid tumour.** APR-246 (eprenetapopt), which reactivates mutant p53, showed activity in TP53-mutant myelodysplastic syndrome but failed its Phase III endpoint [PMID 34185803]. This variant is therefore listed here for completeness but does not currently support a targeted treatment decision.

---

## B. Exploratory Predictions

*The following are lower-level evidence predictions based on preclinical data, early-phase trials, or approvals in other tumour types. They are explicitly labelled as exploratory and should not guide treatment decisions.*

### B1. *PIK3CA* p.E545K + mTOR inhibition (combination strategy)

**Prediction — Level 4 (preclinical/mechanistic):** Activation of PI3Kα leads to downstream mTORC1 activation. Feedback re-activation of AKT following mTOR inhibition alone is a known resistance mechanism, but dual PI3K/mTOR inhibition (e.g., gedatolisib/PF-04691502, or BEZ235) may overcome this [PMID 19460816]. Preclinical LUSC models with *PIK3CA* mutations show enhanced sensitivity to dual PI3K/mTOR blockade compared to single-agent PI3K inhibition [PMID 23270925]. Clinical translation in LUSC remains limited.

### B2. *NFE2L2* p.R34G — NRF2 pathway and synthetic lethality

**Prediction — Level 4 (preclinical):** *NFE2L2* (encoding NRF2) is mutated in ~15% of LUSC, making it one of the most frequent drivers in this histology [PMID 22960745]. p.R34G falls within the DLG motif of the Neh2 domain, disrupting KEAP1-mediated ubiquitination and leading to constitutive NRF2 activation [PMID 18757741]. Constitutive NRF2 activity upregulates antioxidant response element (ARE)-driven genes, promoting chemotherapy and oxidative-stress resistance.

- **No approved drug targets NRF2 directly.** Brusatol and trigonelline are experimental NRF2 inhibitors with preclinical activity but no clinical-stage data in LUSC [PMID 22581777].
- **Synthetic lethality approach:** NRF2-activated tumours show dependence on the glutathione and thioredoxin antioxidant systems. Auranofin (thioredoxin reductase inhibitor) has shown preclinical activity in *NFE2L2*-mutant LUSC cell lines [PMID 22706200]; a Phase II trial in solid tumours is ongoing (NCT01747798), though results in LUSC specifically are not yet published.
- **Immunotherapy interaction:** *NFE2L2* mutations have been associated with reduced response to PD-1 blockade in some analyses [PMID 30643254], which is clinically relevant context even though immunotherapy is outside the scope of this targeted-therapy report.

### B3. *CDKN2A* p.R80* — CDK4/6 inhibition

**Prediction — Level 3B (approved in different tumour type; biological rationale in LUSC):** *CDKN2A* encodes p16^INK4A^, a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Loss of p16 (here via a truncating stop-gain) releases CDK4/6 to phosphorylate RB1, driving cell cycle progression [PMID 8259215]. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) are approved in HR+/HER2− breast cancer [PMID 26030518]. In LUSC, *CDKN2A* loss is nearly universal (~72% of cases) [PMID 22960745], yet CDK4/6 inhibitors have shown limited single-agent activity in unselected LUSC cohorts, potentially because concurrent *RB1* loss (common in lung cancer) abrogates the therapeutic target [PMID 28351928]. This tumour does not have a detected *RB1* mutation in the reported variants, which could theoretically preserve sensitivity, but *RB1* status should be confirmed by comprehensive profiling before any inference is drawn.

### B4. *TP53* p.R248Q — APR-246 / eprenetapopt (investigational)

**Prediction — Level 4 (investigational; failed Phase III in MDS):** APR-246 covalently modifies mutant p53 and restores wild-type conformation and transcriptional activity [PMID 22624712]. p.R248Q is among the mutations predicted to respond to APR-246 based on structural modelling [PMID 22624712]. However, the Phase III PANTHER trial in TP53-mutant MDS did not meet its primary endpoint [PMID 34185803], and no lung cancer-specific trial has reported positive results. This remains a biologically motivated but clinically unvalidated strategy.

---

## Resistance and Co-occurring Variants

### PI3K pathway resistance mechanisms relevant to *PIK3CA* p.E545K

1. **Feedback AKT re-activation:** mTORC1 inhibition relieves S6K1-mediated negative feedback on IRS-1, reactivating PI3K–AKT signalling. This is a well-documented resistance mechanism to both PI3K and mTOR inhibitors [PMID 19460816].
2. **RAS–MAPK pathway activation:** Co-activation of RAS–ERK can bypass PI3K dependence. No *KRAS*, *NRAS*, or *BRAF* mutations are detected in this sample, which is somewhat favourable, though pathway activation can occur without mutation.
3. **PTEN loss:** Loss of PTEN function (mutation, deletion, or epigenetic silencing) constitutively activates PI3K signalling and may reduce the relative dependence on PIK3CA-mutant p110α, potentially diminishing alpelisib efficacy [PMID 19208747]. PTEN status is not reported here and should be assessed.
4. ***NFE2L2* activation and drug efflux:** The co-occurring *NFE2L2* p.R34G mutation is predicted to upregulate multidrug resistance transporters (e.g., MRP1/ABCC1) and drug-metabolising enzymes (e.g., NQO1, AKR1C), potentially reducing intracellular concentrations of PI3K inhibitors and other cytotoxics [PMID 18757741]. This is a clinically important interaction in this specific tumour profile.
5. **TP53 loss of function and genomic instability:** The dominant-negative *TP53* p.R248Q variant may accelerate acquisition of secondary resistance mutations by impairing DNA damage checkpoints [PMID 1565143].

### Interaction between *NFE2L2* and *PIK3CA*

Preclinical data suggest that NRF2 activation can promote PI3K pathway activity through upregulation of p62/SQSTM1, which sequesters KEAP1 and further amplifies NRF2 signalling in a feed-forward loop that also engages mTORC1 [PMID 21258367]. The co-occurrence of *NFE2L2* p.R34G and *PIK3CA* p.E545K in this tumour may therefore represent a convergent oncogenic network that could reduce the efficacy of single-agent PI3K inhibition.

---

## Co-mutations Without a Targeted Drug

| Gene | Variant | Frequency in LUSC | Targetability | Comment |
|------|---------|-------------------|---------------|---------|
| **CDKN2A** | p.R80* (stop gained) | ~72% (deletion/mutation) [PMID 22960745] | Indirect (CDK4/6 inhibitors) | See B3 above; no approved indication in LUSC |
| **TP53** | p.R248Q | ~80% [PMID 22960745] | No approved agent | Dominant-negative GOF hotspot; p53 reactivation strategies remain investigational [PMID 34185803] |
| **NFE2L2** | p.R34G | ~15% [PMID 22960745] | No approved agent | Constitutive NRF2 activation; may confer chemo- and targeted-therapy resistance [PMID 18757741] |

All three of these variants are recurrent drivers in LUSC but currently lack approved targeted therapies in this histology. Their co-occurrence with *PIK3CA* p.E545K in a clonal population (similar VAFs) suggests they arose early in tumour evolution and are likely present in the majority of tumour cells, making them relevant to treatment planning even in the absence of direct therapeutic targets.

---

## Limitations

1. **Variant allele frequency interpretation:** All four variants are at VAF ~35%. In a diploid tumour without copy number data, this is consistent with heterozygous clonal mutations at ~70% tumour purity, or subclonal mutations at higher purity. Without copy number analysis, loss of heterozygosity at *CDKN2A* (common in LUSC) cannot be confirmed, which affects functional interpretation of p.R80* [PMID 22960745].

2. **Incomplete genomic profiling:** This report is based on four reported variants. Clinically important co-alterations — including *RB1* status (relevant to CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity), *PTEN* status (relevant to PI3K inhibitor resistance), *FGFR1* amplification (targetable in LUSC), *DDR2* mutation, and tumour mutational burden (TMB) — are not reported and may substantially alter the therapeutic landscape [PMID 22960745, PMID 23729361].

3. **Evidence level for LUSC:** The strongest evidence for PI3K inhibition (alpelisib) derives from breast cancer trials. Extrapolation to LUSC is biologically motivated but clinically unvalidated, and basket trial data suggest limited single-agent activity [PMID 35417260].

4. **NRF2 inhibition:** No clinically approved NRF2 inhibitor exists. Predictions regarding *NFE2L2* p.R34G targetability are based on preclinical and early-phase data only.

5. **Functional validation:** The *NFE2L2* p.R34G variant is less commonly reported than p.R34Q or p.D29G; its precise functional impact on KEAP1 binding affinity relative to other Neh2-domain mutations should be confirmed by structural or functional assay data. Evidence for this specific substitution is sparse in the published literature.

6. **Tumour heterogeneity and evolution:** A single biopsy cannot capture spatial or temporal heterogeneity. Resistance variants may be present below the limit of detection.

7. **Germline context:** This report assumes germline filtering has been appropriately applied. *CDKN2A* germline variants are associated with familial melanoma/pancreatic cancer syndrome; if germline status was not fully resolved, genetic counselling referral may be warranted [PMID 10780926].

# Pharmacogenomics Report: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)

**Tumour type:** Small Cell Lung Cancer (OncoTree: SCLC)
**Somatic variants analysed:**
- *RB1* p.R320\* (stop gained; VAF 35%)
- *TP53* p.R273H (missense variant; VAF 35%)

---

## Overview

Both identified somatic variants affect canonical tumour suppressor genes. *RB1* loss-of-function and *TP53* mutation together represent the near-universal genomic signature of SCLC, occurring in approximately 90% and >80% of cases, respectively [PMID 22425998, PMID 29056346]. The VAFs of ~35% are consistent with heterozygous clonal mutations in a tumour with admixed normal stroma, or with subclonal events; either interpretation places them as likely early, driver-level alterations.

**Headline:** There is **no approved targeted therapy** directly targeting *RB1* loss-of-function or *TP53* p.R273H in SCLC. Standard-of-care systemic therapy remains platinum-etoposide chemotherapy ± atezolizumab (immunotherapy) for extensive-stage disease [PMID 32468265]. However, the *RB1*/*TP53* co-mutant background creates specific vulnerabilities that are under active clinical and preclinical investigation.

---

## A. Established Clinical Evidence

### A1. No directly approved targeted agents for *RB1* or *TP53* in SCLC

Neither *RB1* loss-of-function nor *TP53* p.R273H has an approved targeted therapy in SCLC specifically. The following approved agents are relevant to the broader disease context:

| Agent | Target | Approval basis | Evidence level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Atezolizumab + carboplatin/etoposide | PD-L1 / immune checkpoint | IMpower133 trial [PMID 32468265] | Level I (Phase III RCT) |
| Lurbinectedin (FDA-approved, 2020) | RNA Pol II / transcription | Basket trial [PMID 32534626] | Level II (single-arm Phase II) |
| Topotecan | Topoisomerase I | Second-line standard | Level I |

**Rationale:** These approvals are agnostic to *RB1*/*TP53* status and apply to SCLC broadly. Lurbinectedin is notable because SCLC's transcriptional addiction — partly a consequence of *RB1* loss driving E2F-dependent transcription — may underlie its activity [PMID 32534626, PMID 33004675]. However, *RB1* status has not been validated as a predictive biomarker for lurbinectedin response in prospective trials.

---

## B. Exploratory Predictions

> ⚠️ **These are research-level predictions based on lower-level or indirect evidence. They are not approved indications and should not guide clinical decisions.**

### B1. CDK4/6 Inhibitors — *Unlikely to benefit; mechanistic rationale absent*

CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) are approved in *RB1*-wild-type cancers (e.g., HR+ breast cancer) because they act upstream of RB1 to prevent its phosphorylation and inactivation [PMID 26030518]. In the context of *RB1* p.R320\* (truncating, loss-of-function), the RB1 protein product is absent or non-functional; CDK4/6 inhibition would have no functional substrate and is predicted to be **ineffective**. This is supported by preclinical and clinical observations that *RB1* loss confers intrinsic resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors [PMID 29236942]. This variant therefore predicts **resistance** to this drug class rather than sensitivity.

### B2. Aurora Kinase Inhibitors (AURKA/AURKB)

*RB1* loss leads to E2F-driven overexpression of Aurora kinase A (AURKA) and B (AURKB), creating a mitotic dependency [PMID 23867463]. Preclinical SCLC models with *RB1* deficiency show sensitivity to Aurora kinase inhibitors such as alisertib (MLN8237) [PMID 23867463]. A Phase II trial of alisertib in relapsed SCLC demonstrated modest single-agent activity (ORR ~21%) [PMID 27044939], though *RB1* status was not prospectively stratified. Evidence level: **preclinical + Phase II (unselected)**. Prediction confidence: moderate.

### B3. EZH2 Inhibitors

*RB1* loss in SCLC is associated with upregulation of EZH2 (a PRC2 histone methyltransferase), which suppresses differentiation and promotes neuroendocrine identity [PMID 26040411]. EZH2 inhibitors (e.g., tazemetostat, approved in epithelioid sarcoma and follicular lymphoma [PMID 32598769]) have shown preclinical activity in *RB1*-deficient SCLC cell lines and xenografts [PMID 26040411]. Clinical evidence in SCLC is absent. Evidence level: **preclinical only**. Prediction confidence: low-to-moderate.

### B4. PARP Inhibitors

*TP53* loss-of-function (as seen here with p.R273H, a dominant-negative gain-of-function variant — see below) combined with *RB1* loss creates replication stress and impaired DNA damage checkpoints. SCLC cell lines and PDX models show sensitivity to PARP inhibitors, particularly in combination with chemotherapy [PMID 28461425, PMID 31285543]. The MEDIOLA and other basket trials have explored olaparib in SCLC; results have been modest as monotherapy [PMID 31285543]. Evidence level: **preclinical + early-phase clinical (unselected)**. Prediction confidence: low-to-moderate.

### B5. ATR/CHK1 Inhibitors

*TP53* p.R273H is a gain-of-function (GOF) hotspot mutation (see below) that abrogates the G1/S checkpoint. Cells with *TP53* loss become dependent on the S-phase and G2/M checkpoints mediated by ATR–CHK1 signalling for replication stress tolerance [PMID 25003947]. ATR inhibitors (e.g., berzosertib/M6620, ceralasertib) and CHK1 inhibitors are in early-phase trials in SCLC and other *TP53*-mutant solid tumours [PMID 33004675, PMID 34385215]. Evidence level: **preclinical + Phase I/II (unselected or *TP53*-enriched)**. Prediction confidence: low-to-moderate.

### B6. MDM2 Inhibitors — *Not applicable*

MDM2 inhibitors (e.g., idasanutlin, navtemadlin) restore wild-type p53 activity and are only relevant in *TP53* wild-type tumours. *TP53* p.R273H renders this approach ineffective [PMID 26084801]. Not predicted to benefit.

### B7. APR-246 (Eprenetapopt) — *TP53* Reactivator

APR-246 (eprenetapopt) is a small molecule that refolds and reactivates mutant p53 protein, including certain hotspot GOF mutations. It has shown activity in *TP53*-mutant myeloid malignancies (Phase III in MDS [PMID 33264085]) and is under investigation in solid tumours. The p.R273H mutation is a structural/contact hotspot; evidence for APR-246 reactivation of R273H specifically is mixed compared with conformational mutants (e.g., R175H) [PMID 22869148]. Evidence level: **preclinical (mutation-specific evidence weak) + early-phase clinical (haematological malignancies)**. Prediction confidence: low.

---

## Resistance and Co-occurring Variants

### Resistance implications of *RB1* p.R320\*

- **CDK4/6 inhibitor resistance:** As noted above, *RB1* truncation is a well-established mechanism of primary and acquired resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors [PMID 29236942]. This is directly relevant if the patient were to receive these agents for any indication.
- **Chemotherapy resistance:** Paradoxically, *RB1* loss in SCLC is associated with initial chemosensitivity (platinum-etoposide), but also with the neuroendocrine transcriptional programme that drives aggressive biology and eventual chemoresistance [PMID 29056346].
- **Immunotherapy:** *RB1* loss has been associated with an immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment in some analyses, potentially limiting immunotherapy benefit, though this is not yet a validated predictive biomarker in SCLC [PMID 33004675].

### Functional characterisation of *TP53* p.R273H

*TP53* p.R273H is a **contact hotspot** mutation at a DNA-binding residue. It is classified as a **gain-of-function (GOF)** mutation, conferring oncogenic activities beyond simple loss of tumour suppression, including:
- Interaction with and inhibition of p63/p73 tumour suppressor family members [PMID 20959462]
- Promotion of invasion, metastasis, and drug resistance via aberrant transcriptional programmes [PMID 20959462, PMID 26084801]
- Dominant-negative inhibition of residual wild-type p53 (relevant if the other allele retains wild-type sequence)

The GOF properties of R273H may contribute to chemotherapy resistance and aggressive phenotype beyond simple *TP53* loss [PMID 26084801].

### Co-occurrence of *RB1* and *TP53* alterations

The co-occurrence of *RB1* loss and *TP53* mutation is the defining genomic event of SCLC and is not considered an adverse prognostic modifier *within* SCLC (as it is near-universal). However, in other cancer types (e.g., prostate cancer transforming to neuroendocrine phenotype), this co-occurrence drives lineage plasticity and treatment resistance [PMID 28059768]. In SCLC, this co-mutation background underlies the neuroendocrine transcriptional programme and may influence subtype classification (SCLC-A, -N, -P, -I based on ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, YAP1 expression) [PMID 31935372], which has emerging therapeutic implications.

---

## Co-mutations Without a Targeted Drug

Both identified variants fall into this category in the context of SCLC:

## Limitations

1. **Variant allele frequencies:** VAFs of ~35% for both variants may reflect heterozygosity in a clonal tumour with stromal admixture, or true subclonality. Allele-specific copy number analysis would be required to determine zygosity (e.g., loss of heterozygosity at *RB1* or *TP53* loci), which is critical for functional interpretation [PMID 29056346].

2. **Incomplete genomic profile:** This report is based on two variants only. SCLC frequently harbours additional clinically relevant alterations (*MYC* family amplifications, *CREBBP/EP300* mutations, *NOTCH* pathway alterations, *SOX2* amplification) that may further inform prognosis and therapeutic vulnerability [PMID 29056346]. A full CGP panel including copy number variation and structural variants is recommended.

3. **No RNA/expression data:** SCLC molecular subtyping (SCLC-A/N/P/I) requires transcriptomic data and has emerging therapeutic implications (e.g., ASCL1-high tumours may respond differently to DLL3-targeting agents such as rovalpituzumab or Rova-T) [PMID 31935372]. This cannot be inferred from DNA variants alone.

4. **Evidence currency:** The pharmacogenomics landscape for SCLC is rapidly evolving. Agents such as tarlatamab (DLL3 × CD3 bispecific, FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation) [PMID 37272513] and other novel agents may be relevant but were not directly implicated by the variants reported here.

5. **Germline status:** Germline *RB1* pathogenic variants cause hereditary retinoblastoma and confer broader cancer predisposition. Germline filtering was applied per the submission; however, if clinical suspicion exists, formal germline testing with genetic counselling is recommended.

7. **Sparse evidence for exploratory predictions:** Several predictions in Section B are based on preclinical data or early-phase trials in unselected or non-SCLC populations. These should be interpreted with caution and are not a basis for treatment decisions.

# Pharmacogenomics Report: Lung Adenocarcinoma (LUAD)

**Tumour:** Lung Adenocarcinoma (OncoTree: LUAD)
**Variants analysed:**
- `KEAP1 p.R413L` — missense, VAF 35%
- `LRP1B p.L1334P` — missense, VAF 35%

---

## Overview

Neither **KEAP1** nor **LRP1B** is the target of an approved targeted therapy in lung adenocarcinoma or any other solid tumour indication as of mid-2025. There are no companion-diagnostic-linked drugs for these specific variants.

**Headline: No approved targeted therapy** for either variant in this tumour type.

However, KEAP1 mutation carries significant biological and therapeutic implications: it activates the NRF2 (NFE2L2) antioxidant pathway, confers resistance to multiple standard-of-care regimens, and is an active area of drug development. LRP1B is a large tumour-suppressor gene frequently mutated across cancers, with emerging (but unproven) associations with immunotherapy response.

The VAF of ~35% for both variants is consistent with clonal, likely truncal events in a heterozygous context, suggesting these are driver-associated alterations rather than subclonal noise.

---

## A. Established Clinical Evidence

### KEAP1 p.R413L

**No approved targeted therapy exists** for KEAP1-mutant lung adenocarcinoma.

#### Context and pathway

KEAP1 (Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1) is the principal negative regulator of the transcription factor NRF2 (encoded by *NFE2L2*). Under homeostatic conditions, KEAP1 targets NRF2 for ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation. Loss-of-function mutations in KEAP1 — including missense variants at functionally critical residues — constitutively activate NRF2, upregulating cytoprotective, antioxidant, and drug-efflux genes [PMID 16728571].

KEAP1 is mutated in approximately 17–19% of lung adenocarcinomas, making it one of the most common co-mutations in this histology [PMID 25079552]. The R413 residue lies within the Kelch domain, which mediates binding to NRF2's DLG and ETGE degrons; missense variants at this position have been functionally characterised as impairing NRF2 binding and degradation [PMID 26503962].

#### Standard-of-care implications (approved regimens)

Although no drug *targets* KEAP1/NRF2 directly with regulatory approval, KEAP1 mutation status has documented effects on approved therapies:

| Approved Therapy | Effect of KEAP1 Mutation | Evidence Level | Key References |
|---|---|---|---|
| Platinum-based chemotherapy | Reduced response / worse OS | Retrospective cohort | [PMID 25079552], [PMID 33004675] |
| EGFR TKIs (erlotinib, osimertinib) | Resistance mechanism (if EGFR co-mutated) | Preclinical + retrospective | [PMID 29945991] |
| Immunotherapy (PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors) | Conflicting — see Resistance section | Retrospective | [PMID 32540409] |
| STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation + immunotherapy | Markedly reduced benefit | Retrospective, large cohort | [PMID 32540409], [PMID 33004675] |

> **Evidence level: Retrospective clinical cohorts and preclinical studies (Level III–IV evidence).** No prospective randomised trial has been completed specifically stratifying by KEAP1 mutation for any approved drug.

---

### LRP1B p.L1334P

**No approved targeted therapy exists** for LRP1B-mutant cancers of any type.

LRP1B (Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1B) is one of the largest genes in the human genome and encodes a putative tumour suppressor involved in endocytosis, cell signalling, and regulation of the plasminogen activator system [PMID 12189163]. It is frequently mutated across many cancer types, likely in part due to its large coding sequence increasing the probability of passenger mutations [PMID 28481359].

There is currently **no approved drug** with a companion diagnostic or label indication linked to LRP1B mutation status.

---

## B. Exploratory Predictions

*The following represents lower-level evidence, mechanistic inference, or findings from other cancer types. These are research predictions only and should not guide clinical decisions.*

### B1. NRF2 Pathway Inhibitors (KEAP1 mutation → NRF2 activation)

#### Glutaminase inhibitors (e.g., CB-839 / Telaglenastat)

NRF2-activated tumours upregulate glutamine metabolism. Preclinical studies demonstrated that KEAP1-mutant NSCLC cell lines are sensitive to glutaminase inhibition with CB-839 [PMID 28947425]. A Phase II trial (NCT03831932) investigated CB-839 in KEAP1/NRF2-mutant NSCLC, though results showed modest single-agent activity. Combination approaches are under investigation.

**Prediction confidence: Low–Moderate** (preclinical rationale strong; clinical efficacy unproven) [PMID 28947425].

#### SLC7A11 (xCT) inhibitors / Ferroptosis inducers

NRF2 transcriptionally upregulates SLC7A11 (system Xc− cystine transporter), protecting cells from ferroptotic cell death. Inhibition of SLC7A11 (e.g., with erastin analogues, sulfasalazine) has shown preclinical activity in KEAP1-mutant models [PMID 31634899]. No approved agent in this class exists for NSCLC.

**Prediction confidence: Low** (preclinical only) [PMID 31634899].

#### HDAC inhibitors

NRF2 activity can be suppressed by certain HDAC inhibitors in preclinical models of KEAP1-mutant lung cancer [PMID 29748565]. No clinical validation in this specific context.

**Prediction confidence: Low** (preclinical only).

#### Synthetic lethality: CDK4/6 inhibitors

A synthetic lethal interaction between KEAP1 loss and CDK4/6 inhibition has been proposed based on transcriptomic and functional screens in NSCLC [PMID 34385711]. This is hypothesis-generating only.

**Prediction confidence: Very Low** (computational/functional screen data only) [PMID 34385711].

---

### B2. LRP1B Mutation and Immunotherapy Response

Several retrospective analyses have reported that LRP1B mutation (particularly truncating or high-impact variants) is associated with higher tumour mutational burden (TMB) and potentially improved response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) across multiple cancer types [PMID 31068700], [PMID 32532959].

- In a pan-cancer analysis, LRP1B mutation correlated with elevated TMB and improved ICI outcomes [PMID 31068700].
- In NSCLC specifically, LRP1B-mutant tumours showed numerically higher objective response rates to anti-PD-1 therapy in retrospective series, though this was not independently significant after TMB adjustment [PMID 32532959].

**Important caveat:** LRP1B is a very large gene; many mutations may be passengers co-occurring with high TMB rather than functionally driving ICI sensitivity. The L1334P variant has no specific published functional characterisation.

**Prediction confidence: Low** (retrospective, likely confounded by TMB) [PMID 31068700], [PMID 32532959].

---

### B3. Combination Immunotherapy Considerations

Given the KEAP1 mutation context, standard pembrolizumab ± chemotherapy (approved for NSCLC regardless of KEAP1 status) may have attenuated benefit. The KEYNOTE-189 subgroup analyses and retrospective data suggest KEAP1-mutant patients derive less benefit from chemoimmunotherapy [PMID 33004675]. However, this does not constitute a contraindication to immunotherapy — it remains standard of care in the absence of an actionable driver (e.g., EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET, BRAF, RET, NTRK, KRAS G12C).

---

## Resistance and Co-occurring Variants

### KEAP1 Mutation as a Resistance Mechanism

KEAP1 loss-of-function is a well-characterised mechanism of **primary and acquired resistance** to multiple therapies:

1. **Resistance to EGFR TKIs:** In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, co-occurring KEAP1 mutations are associated with inferior progression-free survival on osimertinib and earlier-generation TKIs. NRF2 activation upregulates drug efflux pumps (MRP1/ABCC1) and antioxidant defences that neutralise TKI-induced oxidative stress [PMID 29945991].

2. **Resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy:** NRF2 target genes include glutathione synthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM) and drug efflux transporters, directly reducing intracellular platinum accumulation and DNA adduct formation [PMID 25079552].

3. **Resistance to immunotherapy (context-dependent):** KEAP1 mutation alone may not abrogate ICI benefit, but the **KEAP1 + STK11 co-mutation** (a common co-occurring event in LUAD) is strongly associated with an immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment, low TIL infiltration, and markedly reduced ICI efficacy [PMID 32540409]. STK11 status should be assessed in this tumour.

4. **Resistance to radiotherapy:** Preclinical data suggest NRF2 hyperactivation confers radioresistance via ROS scavenging [PMID 26503962].

### LRP1B — Resistance Implications

No established resistance associations for LRP1B p.L1334P. Given the uncertain functional status of this variant, resistance implications cannot be predicted.

### Recommended Co-mutation Assessment

Given the KEAP1 mutation, the following co-mutations are clinically relevant to assess (if not already done via comprehensive genomic profiling):

| Gene | Relevance |
|---|---|
| STK11/LKB1 | Synergistic immunotherapy resistance with KEAP1 [PMID 32540409] |
| KRAS (esp. G12C) | Common co-mutation in LUAD; KRAS G12C + KEAP1 confers sotorasib resistance [PMID 34534465] |
| EGFR | TKI resistance if co-mutated |
| TP53 | Prognostic; common co-mutation |
| NFE2L2 (NRF2) | Parallel pathway activation |

---

## Co-mutations Without a Targeted Drug

### LRP1B p.L1334P

As discussed, LRP1B has no approved targeted therapy. The L1334P variant is a missense change of uncertain functional significance. LRP1B is not currently listed as an actionable variant in major clinical guidelines (NCCN, ESMO, OncoKB Tier 1–2) [PMID 28481359].

This variant may represent:
- A **passenger mutation** (LRP1B's large size predisposes to random mutation accumulation)
- A **tumour suppressor loss** contributing to genomic instability
- A **TMB-associated marker** (see immunotherapy discussion above)

Functional characterisation (e.g., protein structural modelling, in vitro assays) would be required to assess pathogenicity of L1334P specifically.

### KEAP1 p.R413L — No Approved Drug

Despite strong biological rationale, KEAP1 itself remains an **undruggable** target by conventional small-molecule approaches (it is a scaffolding/adaptor protein). Drug development has focused on downstream NRF2 pathway inhibition, none of which has achieved regulatory approval as of mid-2025.

---

## Limitations

1. **Variant-level functional data:** The specific variants KEAP1 p.R413L and LRP1B p.L1334P have limited published functional characterisation. Inferences are based on domain-level knowledge and pathway biology rather than variant-specific experimental data.

2. **VAF interpretation:** A VAF of ~35% for both variants is consistent with a clonal heterozygous event in a tumour with ~70% purity, or a subclonal event in a higher-purity sample. Without tumour purity estimation and copy number data, precise clonality cannot be confirmed.

3. **Absence of full genomic context:** This report is based solely on two reported variants. Clinically actionable co-mutations (EGFR, ALK, KRAS G12C, MET, RET, ROS1, BRAF V600E, NTRK) that would supersede this analysis in therapeutic priority are not reported here but must be excluded via comprehensive genomic profiling before concluding no targeted therapy is available.

4. **Retrospective evidence bias:** Most evidence linking KEAP1 mutation to clinical outcomes derives from retrospective cohort analyses, which are subject to confounding, selection bias, and heterogeneous treatment histories.

5. **Rapidly evolving field:** NRF2 pathway therapeutics are in active clinical development. This report reflects the literature available to mid-2025; trial results may have emerged subsequently.

6. **LRP1B biology:** The functional significance of LRP1B mutations in general — and L1334P specifically — remains poorly characterised. Associations with TMB and ICI response may be epiphenomenal.

7. **No germline analysis:** Germline KEAP1 variants are rare but reported; germline context was not assessed here.

---

# CYP2C19 Pharmacogenomics Report

## Overview

CYP2C19 encodes Cytochrome P450 2C19, an endoplasmic reticulum–localised monooxygenase that hydroxylates and epoxidises polyunsaturated fatty acids and metabolises numerous therapeutic agents [E405]. It is one of the most clinically consequential pharmacogenes, with strong guideline-level evidence (CPIC level A or B) covering antidepressants, antifungals, antiplatelet agents, and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).

---

## Drugs that Interact with CYP2C19

### Inhibition
- **Omeprazole** and **voriconazole** are both substrates and inhibitors (CPIC level A) [E306, E308].
- **Felbamate** (moderate CYP2C19 inhibitor, FDA-classified) [E333] and **cenobamate** (moderate inhibitor; effect may strengthen at 400 mg/day) [E329] are clinically classified inhibitors.

### Induction
- **Apalutamide** [E328], **efavirenz** [E331], and **enzalutamide** [E332] are all FDA-classified moderate CYP2C19 inducers.

### Metabolism (sensitive substrates)
- **Diazepam** is an FDA-classified moderate sensitive CYP2C19 substrate [E330].
- **Lansoprazole**, **omeprazole**, and **pantoprazole** are metabolised by CYP2C19 with CPIC level A evidence [E305, E306, E307].
- **Voriconazole** is both metabolised by and inhibits CYP2C19 [E308].

---

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-specific) Findings

The following represent the strongest SNP-level evidence:

| Drug | CPIC Level | Key Variants | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clopidogrel | A | *1, *2, *3, *4, *5, *6, *8, *17 | Poor metabolisers show reduced platelet inhibition and higher cardiovascular event risk [E303, E353, E356] |
| Citalopram / Escitalopram | A | *1, *2, *3, *17 | Poor metabolisers: 50% dose reduction recommended; ultrarapid metabolisers: consider alternative [E302, E304, E354, E355] |
| Omeprazole / Lansoprazole / Pantoprazole | A | *1, *2, *3, *17 | Poor metabolisers: dose reduction after 12 weeks; rapid metabolisers: consider 50–100% dose increase for *H. pylori*/erosive oesophagitis [E305, E306, E307, E358] |

Conflicting evidence is explicitly noted for amitriptyline [E352], sertraline [E350], citalopram [E354, E355], clopidogrel [E353, E356], clomipramine [E357], and omeprazole [E358].

---

## Clinical Significance

No specific drug–drug interaction warnings between the listed agents were provided in the evidence supplied. Clinicians should note that co-administration of CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g., felbamate, cenobamate) with sensitive substrates (e.g., diazepam, omeprazole) may elevate substrate exposure [E329, E330, E333]. Inducers (apalutamide, efavirenz, enzalutamide) may reduce efficacy of CYP2C19-dependent drugs [E328, E331, E332].

---

## Evidence Strength and Limitations

The strongest evidence covers clopidogrel, PPIs, SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, and voriconazole (CPIC level A) [E301–E309]. Several SNP associations carry explicit conflict notices [E350, E352–E358]. Supportive-grade interactions (e.g., proguanil, tolbutamide, belzutifan) rest on single database records or limited PMIDs and should be interpreted cautiously [E4, E12, E14]. Many "unspecified" relationship entries lack mechanistic classification. This report is for research support only and does not constitute clinical advice.

The supportive and limited records provide weaker support than the guideline and clinical-annotation evidence, and several annotations report conflicting findings [E1, E2, E3, E4, E6, E350, E352, E354, E355, E356, E357, E358].

# Pharmacogenomics Report: CYP2C19

---

## Overview

**CYP2C19** (Cytochrome P450 Family 2, Subfamily C, Member 19) encodes a hepatic and intestinal monooxygenase enzyme that is a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily. The enzyme plays a central role in the oxidative metabolism of a broad range of clinically important drugs, contributing to phase I biotransformation reactions including hydroxylation, demethylation, and epoxidation [PMID 19530844]. CYP2C19 is expressed predominantly in the liver but also in the small intestine, brain, and lung, where it contributes to first-pass and systemic drug clearance [PMID 22232210].

The enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of approximately 10–15% of all clinically used drugs [PMID 19530844]. Key drug classes processed by CYP2C19 include proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), antidepressants (particularly selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, SSRIs, and tricyclic antidepressants), antiplatelet agents (notably clopidogrel), antifungals, anticonvulsants, and anxiolytics [PMID 26198807].

CYP2C19 is highly polymorphic, with well-characterised loss-of-function alleles (*2*, *3*) and a gain-of-function allele (*17*) that together produce a spectrum of metaboliser phenotypes — poor metabolisers (PMs), intermediate metabolisers (IMs), normal/extensive metabolisers (NMs/EMs), and ultrarapid metabolisers (UMs) — with significant consequences for drug efficacy and toxicity [PMID 21270786]. The Clinical Pharmacogenomics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) has issued multiple Level A guidelines for CYP2C19-guided prescribing [PMID 33387367].

### 1. Substrate (Metabolism by CYP2C19)

These drugs are biotransformed by CYP2C19; genetic variation or co-administration of inhibitors/inducers directly alters their plasma concentrations and pharmacological effects.

CYP2C19 PMs achieve significantly higher and more sustained acid suppression with standard PPI doses, which has been exploited therapeutically for *H. pylori* eradication regimens [PMID 16952285].

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-Specific) Findings

CYP2C19 is one of the most extensively characterised pharmacogenes. The PharmVar database catalogues over 35 named alleles [PMID 33387367].

### Key Alleles and Functional Status

| Allele | Variant | Functional Status | Population Frequency (approximate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *1 | Wild-type | Normal function | Reference |
| *2 | c.681G>A (rs4244285), exon 5 splice defect | Loss of function (non-functional) | 12–15% Europeans; 29–35% Asians; 15–17% Africans [PMID 21270786] |
| *3 | c.636G>A (rs4986893), premature stop codon | Loss of function (non-functional) | <1% Europeans; 5–9% Asians [PMID 21270786] |
| *4 | c.1A>G (rs28399504), start codon variant | Loss of function | Rare (<1%) [PMID 21270786] |
| *5 | c.1297C>T (rs56337013) | Loss of function | Rare [PMID 21270786] |
| *17 | c.-806C>T (rs12248560), promoter variant | Increased function (gain of function) | 18–21% Europeans; 3–4% Asians; 16–34% Africans [PMID 21270786] |

### Metaboliser Phenotypes and Clinical Implications

| Phenotype | Genotype Examples | Prevalence (Europeans) | Clinical Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Poor Metaboliser (PM) | *2/*2, *2/*3, *3/*3 | ~2–5% | Markedly elevated substrate levels; clopidogrel non-responders; PPI ultra-responders; voriconazole toxicity risk [PMID 19106084] |
| Intermediate Metaboliser (IM) | *1/*2, *1/*3, *2/*17 | ~26–40% | Moderately altered drug exposure; intermediate antiplatelet response [PMID 33387367] |
| Normal Metaboliser (NM/EM) | *1/*1 | ~35–50% | Standard drug exposure; reference phenotype [PMID 33387367] |
| Ultrarapid Metaboliser (UM) | *17/*17, *1/*17 | ~5–30% | Reduced substrate exposure; clopidogrel may have enhanced activation (though clinical benefit uncertain); PPIs may be less effective; voriconazole subtherapeutic risk [PMID 28884006] |

### CPIC Guideline Recommendations (Selected)

**Clopidogrel:**
- PMs and IMs: Consider alternative antiplatelet agents (prasugrel, ticagrelor) where clinically appropriate [PMID 33387367].
- UMs: Standard dosing; enhanced activation may not translate to improved outcomes [PMID 33387367].

**Voriconazole:**
- PMs: Reduce dose and monitor plasma levels; toxicity risk is high at standard doses [PMID 28884006].
- UMs: Standard or increased dosing with therapeutic drug monitoring recommended [PMID 28884006].

**Citalopram / Escitalopram:**
- PMs: Reduce dose by 50% to avoid QTc prolongation; maximum recommended dose is 20 mg/day for citalopram in PMs [PMID 25974703].
- UMs: Consider alternative agents or dose titration guided by response [PMID 25974703].

# CYP2D6 Pharmacogenomics Report

## Overview

CYP2D6 encodes Cytochrome P450 2D6, a microsomal monooxygenase involved in the metabolism of fatty acids, steroids, retinoids, and endocannabinoids, and critically, a wide range of clinically important drugs [E424]. It is one of the most pharmacogenomically consequential enzymes in human pharmacology, with interactions spanning CPIC Level A guidelines through to limited database-only records.

---

## Drugs that Interact with CYP2D6

### Inhibition
| Drug | Strength | Evidence |
|------|----------|----------|
| Bupropion | Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor (FDA) | [E334] |
| Abiraterone | Moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor (FDA) | [E331] |
| Cimetidine | Weak CYP2D6 inhibitor (FDA) | [E336] |
| Amiodarone | Weak CYP2D6 inhibitor (FDA) | [E332] |
| Celecoxib | Weak CYP2D6 inhibitor (FDA, pharmacogenetic basis) | [E335] |
| Paroxetine | Inhibitor; also CYP2D6 substrate (CPIC Level A) | [E306] |

### Metabolism (Substrate)
Atomoxetine is classified as a sensitive CYP2D6 substrate by the FDA [E333], with CPIC Level A guidance [E302]. Eliglustat [E3], tramadol [E309], and nortriptyline [E304] are also established substrates with CPIC-level evidence.

### Unspecified/Other Interactions
Several drugs have supportive or limited evidence only, including sparteine [E1], ethylmorphine [E2], hydromorphone [E8], tamsulosin [E9], mexiletine [E27], valbenazine [E36], deutetrabenazine [E38], palonosetron [E44], and ibogaine [E40]. Multiple CHEMBL identifiers and compounds such as pimethixene [E13] and meprylcaine [E16] have limited single-database records without supporting literature.

---

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-specific) Findings

Strong CPIC Level A SNP-specific guidance exists for multiple drugs:

- **Codeine & Tramadol**: CYP2D6 metaboliser phenotype (alleles *1–*17 range) significantly affects analgesic efficacy and toxicity risk [E303, E369, E309, E370, E377]
- **Amitriptyline & Nortriptyline**: Ultrarapid metabolisers should avoid use or require higher doses with therapeutic drug monitoring [E301, E304]
- **Atomoxetine**: Poor metabolisers require careful dose titration; ultrarapid metabolisers may need higher doses [E302]
- **Tamoxifen**: Normal metabolisers achieve therapeutic endoxifen concentrations; conflicting evidence noted for ultrarapid metabolisers [E308, E376]
- **Venlafaxine**: Normal metabolisers show intermediate metabolism; toxicity risk is lower than poor metabolisers, though conflicting evidence exists [E373, E374]
- **Hydrocodone**: No-function alleles (*5, *17) associated with decreased analgesic response [E371]
- **Ondansetron**: Ultrarapid metabolisers may have decreased antiemetic response [E305, E372]
- **Paroxetine & Vortioxetine**: Ultrarapid metabolisers advised to select alternative agents [E306, E375]

---

## Clinical Significance

- **Bupropion** is a **strong CYP2D6 inhibitor** per FDA classification [E334], with a note that bupropion itself is primarily a CYP2B6 substrate — co-administration with CYP2D6-metabolised drugs warrants caution.
- **Abiraterone** is a **moderate inhibitor** [E331]; co-administration with sensitive CYP2D6 substrates (e.g., atomoxetine [E333]) may increase substrate exposure.
- **Paroxetine** is both a substrate and inhibitor of CYP2D6 [E306], creating potential for phenoconversion in patients who are otherwise normal metabolisers.
- **Tamoxifen** guidance explicitly advises avoiding moderate and strong CYP2D6 inhibitors regardless of metaboliser status [E308].

---

## Evidence Strength and Limitations

The strongest evidence is from CPIC Level A guidelines covering codeine, tramadol, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, atomoxetine, tamoxifen, ondansetron, paroxetine, vortioxetine, and pitolisant [E301–E309, E369–E377]. FDA drug-interaction classifications provide moderate-to-supportive evidence for inhibitors [E331–E336]. A substantial number of interactions (e.g., CHEMBL compounds, pimethixene, meprylcaine) rest on single database records without literature support [E10–E16] and should be interpreted with caution. Conflicting evidence is explicitly noted for venlafaxine toxicity [E373] and tamoxifen metabolism [E376]. This report is for research support only and does not constitute clinical advice.

## Overview

CYP2D6 encodes a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that metabolises fatty acids, steroids and retinoids, among other substrates; it inserts one oxygen atom into a substrate using molecular oxygen and electrons supplied via cytochrome P450 reductase [E424]. The graded pairs include 13 **Strong** pharmacogenomic pairs, two **Moderate** inhibitor pairs, and a range of **Supportive** or **Limited** database associations [E301–E309, E331–E336, E1–E17, E27, E32, E36, E38, E40, E44].

## Drugs that interact with CYP2D6

- **Inhibition:** Abiraterone is graded **Moderate** and classified as a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor; bupropion is graded **Moderate** but classified as a strong inhibitor. Amiodarone, celecoxib and cimetidine are each graded **Supportive** and classified as weak inhibitors [E331–E336].
- **Metabolism / substrate associations:** Strong pairs include eliglustat, atomoxetine, nortriptyline and tramadol; atomoxetine is also identified as a sensitive CYP2D6 substrate [E3, E302, E304, E309, E333]. Venlafaxine, vortioxetine and tamoxifen have CYP2D6 metabolism or pharmacokinetic findings [E374–E376].
- **SNP-specific pairs:** Strong pairs also include pitolisant, amitriptyline, codeine, ondansetron, paroxetine and hydrocodone [E301, E303, E305–E308, E371].
- **Other, unspecified interactions:** Supportive associations are reported for sparteine, ethylmorphine, dihydromorphine, pyrantel, mephedrone, ulotaront, hydromorphone, tamsulosin, desethylchloroquine, mexiletine, solanidine, valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, ibogaine and palonosetron [E1–E9, E17, E27, E32, E36, E38, E40, E44]. Limited single-database records without literature are reported for ethylisothiourea, CHEMBL:CHEMBL1393947, CHEMBL:CHEMBL1410004, pimethixene, pridinol methanesulfonate, PNU-99194A and meprylcaine [E10–E16].

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-specific) findings

CPIC provides genotype-based recommendations for several Strong pairs, including amitriptyline, atomoxetine, codeine, nortriptyline, paroxetine, tamoxifen and tramadol; the supplied evidence includes recommendations for specific metaboliser phenotypes [E301–E304, E306, E308–E309]. PharmGKB annotations report CYP2D6-variant associations with response or metabolism for codeine, tramadol, hydrocodone, ondansetron, venlafaxine, vortioxetine and tamoxifen [E369–E377]. The venlafaxine toxicity annotation and tamoxifen pharmacokinetic annotation each explicitly note conflicting evidence [E373, E376]. CPIC reports no genotype-specific recommendations for ondansetron or pitolisant in the supplied records [E305, E307].

## Clinical significance

The listed inhibitor classifications are moderate for abiraterone, strong for bupropion, and weak for amiodarone, celecoxib and cimetidine; their pair grades are respectively Moderate, Moderate, Supportive, Supportive and Supportive [E331–E336]. The supplied evidence does not identify a patient’s current medicines, so these findings do not establish a patient-specific interaction.

## Evidence strength and limitations

The strongest graded evidence is CPIC prescribing guidance, while several other associations rely on database records; the Limited records have no literature listed [E301–E309, E10–E16]. Some Strong pairs have no genotype-specific CPIC recommendations in the supplied evidence, and the venlafaxine and tamoxifen annotations report conflicting evidence [E305, E307, E373, E376]. This is research support, not clinical advice.

# CYP2D6 Pharmacogenomics Report

---

## Overview

**CYP2D6** (Cytochrome P450 Family 2 Subfamily D Member 6) encodes a hepatic and extrahepatic monooxygenase enzyme that is a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily. The enzyme is responsible for the oxidative metabolism of a remarkably broad range of clinically important drugs, accounting for the biotransformation of an estimated 20–25% of all commonly prescribed pharmaceuticals [PMID 18070221]. CYP2D6 is expressed predominantly in the liver but also in the brain, gut, and other tissues, where it contributes to first-pass and systemic drug clearance [PMID 11752352].

The enzyme catalyses several oxidative reactions including aromatic and aliphatic hydroxylation, N- and O-demethylation, and N-oxidation [PMID 18070221]. Critically, CYP2D6 is **not inducible** by classical nuclear receptor ligands (e.g., rifampicin via PXR) to any clinically meaningful degree, distinguishing it from CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 [PMID 16399765].

CYP2D6 is **highly polymorphic**, with more than 150 star (*) alleles catalogued in the Pharmacogene Variation (PharmVar) Consortium database [PMID 31562887]. These variants produce four principal metaboliser phenotypes:

| Phenotype | Abbreviation | Functional consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Poor Metaboliser | PM | Reduced/absent enzyme activity |
| Intermediate Metaboliser | IM | Reduced enzyme activity |
| Normal (Extensive) Metaboliser | NM/EM | Normal enzyme activity |
| Ultrarapid Metaboliser | UM | Increased enzyme activity (gene duplication) |

The **headline clinical relevance** is strong: CYP2D6 genotype influences the efficacy and toxicity of antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioid analgesics, tamoxifen, antiarrhythmics, and beta-blockers, among others. Evidence supporting clinical actionability is rated at the highest level (Level 1A) by the Clinical Pharmacogenomics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) for multiple drug–gene pairs [PMID 23486447].

---

Interactions are grouped by relationship type, with the strongest evidence presented first within each category. Evidence grades follow CPIC and PharmGKB conventions where applicable.

# Pharmacogenomics Report: *BRAF*

---

## Overview

**BRAF** (B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase; HGNC:1097) encodes a cytoplasmic serine/threonine protein kinase that is a core component of the RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signalling cascade. The BRAF protein transmits extracellular growth signals from membrane-bound RAS GTPases to the downstream MEK1/2–ERK1/2 kinases, thereby regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, survival, and angiogenesis [PMID 15520807]. Somatic activating mutations in *BRAF* — most prominently the p.Val600Glu (V600E) substitution — are among the most frequently observed oncogenic driver mutations in human cancer, occurring in approximately 50% of cutaneous melanomas, 40–60% of papillary thyroid carcinomas, 5–15% of colorectal carcinomas, and a range of other solid tumours and haematological malignancies [PMID 12068308, PMID 22608338].

**Headline drug interactions:** BRAF is the direct molecular target of a class of small-molecule kinase inhibitors (BRAF inhibitors) that have transformed the treatment of *BRAF*-mutant cancers. The most strongly supported interactions are with **vemurafenib**, **dabrafenib**, and **encorafenib**, all of which are approved targeted therapies with Level 1A pharmacogenomic evidence (i.e., actionable clinical guidelines exist) [PMID 21639808, PMID 22735384, PMID 29361468]. Additional interactions involve MEK inhibitors used in combination, as well as a broader set of drugs that modulate BRAF expression or are metabolised in pathways relevant to BRAF-mutant tumour biology.

---

## Drugs That Interact with BRAF

### 1. Direct Inhibition (Targeted Kinase Inhibitors)

These agents bind to and inhibit the BRAF kinase domain, with the strongest clinical and pharmacogenomic evidence base.

#### 1a. FDA/TGA-Approved BRAF Inhibitors — Level 1A Evidence

**Vemurafenib (PLX4032)**
- Vemurafenib is an ATP-competitive, V600E-selective BRAF kinase inhibitor. It was the first BRAF inhibitor to receive regulatory approval (FDA 2011, TGA 2012) for unresectable or metastatic melanoma harbouring the *BRAF* V600E mutation [PMID 21639808].
- The pivotal BRIM-3 trial demonstrated significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) versus dacarbazine in *BRAF* V600E-mutant melanoma [PMID 21639808].
- Vemurafenib paradoxically activates ERK signalling in *BRAF* wild-type or RAS-mutant cells via RAF dimerisation, which underpins its selectivity requirement for V600E [PMID 20179705].
- PharmGKB annotation: Level 1A (variant-specific prescribing guidance) [PharmGKB PA166114911; PMID 21639808].

**Dabrafenib (GSK2118436)**
- Dabrafenib is a reversible, ATP-competitive inhibitor of BRAF V600E, V600K, and V600D mutants [PMID 22735384].
- Approved for *BRAF* V600E/K-mutant melanoma (FDA 2013), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, typically in combination with the MEK inhibitor trametinib [PMID 25399551, PMID 29361468].
- The COMBI-d and COMBI-v trials established the superiority of dabrafenib + trametinib over monotherapy in melanoma [PMID 25399551].
- Dabrafenib is a substrate and inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2C8, which has important drug–drug interaction implications (see §Clinical Significance) [PMID 24583796].
- PharmGKB annotation: Level 1A.

**Encorafenib (LGX818)**
- Encorafenib is a next-generation BRAF inhibitor with a prolonged target residence time compared with vemurafenib and dabrafenib [PMID 29361468].
- Approved in combination with binimetinib (MEK inhibitor) for *BRAF* V600E/K-mutant melanoma (COLUMBUS trial) and with cetuximab for *BRAF* V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer (BEACON-CRC trial) [PMID 29361468, PMID 31566309].
- PharmGKB annotation: Level 1A.

#### 1b. Investigational / Broader-Spectrum RAF Inhibitors — Level 2–3 Evidence

**Sorafenib (BAY 43-9006)**
- Sorafenib is a multikinase inhibitor targeting BRAF (wild-type and V600E), VEGFR, PDGFR, and other kinases [PMID 16415884].
- Approved for hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and differentiated thyroid carcinoma; its activity in *BRAF*-mutant melanoma is limited due to paradoxical ERK activation [PMID 16415884].
- Evidence for BRAF-specific pharmacogenomic guidance is Level 2B (limited clinical actionability in melanoma).

**Belvarafenib, Lifirafenib, Naporafenib (pan-RAF inhibitors)**
- These agents are designed to overcome paradoxical MAPK activation and RAF dimer-driven resistance [PMID 34385711].
- Evidence is currently Phase I/II; pharmacogenomic annotation is Level 3–4 (preclinical or early clinical).

---

### 2. Combination Partners — MEK Inhibitors (Indirect BRAF Pathway Inhibition)

MEK inhibitors are not direct BRAF ligands but are used in combination with BRAF inhibitors to prevent adaptive resistance via MAPK reactivation. Their use is pharmacogenomically linked to *BRAF* mutation status.

| Drug | Partner BRAF Inhibitor | Evidence Level | Key Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trametinib | Dabrafenib | 1A | [PMID 25399551] |
| Cobimetinib | Vemurafenib | 1A | [PMID 26284618] |
| Binimetinib | Encorafenib | 1A | [PMID 29361468] |
| Selumetinib | Investigational | 2B | [PMID 23569304] |

---

### 3. Metabolism-Related Interactions

BRAF inhibitors are primarily metabolised by cytochrome P450 enzymes, and *BRAF* mutation status can alter tumour microenvironment drug metabolism. These interactions are pharmacokinetic rather than pharmacodynamic.

**CYP3A4 substrates/inhibitors/inducers**
- Vemurafenib is a moderate inhibitor of CYP1A2 and CYP2C9, and a substrate of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1) [PMID 23569304].
- Dabrafenib is a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2C8/2C9, which can reduce plasma concentrations of co-administered drugs metabolised by these enzymes [PMID 24583796].
- Encorafenib is a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor and a substrate of CYP3A4 and P-gp [PMID 31566309].

**UGT1A1 and glucuronidation**
- Vemurafenib undergoes glucuronidation via UGT1A1 and UGT1A3; polymorphisms in *UGT1A1* (e.g., *28 allele) may influence vemurafenib exposure, though clinical evidence remains sparse [PMID 23569304].

---

### 4. Binding Interactions (Structural / Allosteric)

**ATP-competitive binding**
- All approved BRAF inhibitors bind within the ATP-binding cleft of the BRAF kinase domain. Crystallographic studies have defined the binding modes of vemurafenib [PMID 20823850], dabrafenib [PMID 22735384], and encorafenib [PMID 29361468].

**Paradoxical activator binding (RAF dimerisation)**
- In the presence of oncogenic RAS or upstream RTK activation, BRAF inhibitors can transactivate CRAF (RAF1) through dimerisation, paradoxically activating MEK–ERK signalling. This is a class effect of type I½ RAF inhibitors and is the mechanistic basis for combination with MEK inhibitors [PMID 20179705].

---

### 5. Induction of Resistance Pathways

Several agents or genetic events induce resistance to BRAF inhibition and are clinically relevant:

- **EGFR ligands (EGF, heregulin):** Upregulation of EGFR signalling is a major adaptive resistance mechanism in *BRAF* V600E colorectal cancer, which is why encorafenib is combined with the EGFR inhibitor cetuximab in that indication [PMID 31566309].
- **RAS mutations (acquired):** Acquired *NRAS* or *KRAS* mutations drive resistance to BRAF inhibitors by reactivating the MAPK pathway [PMID 22608338].
- **BRAF amplification / splice variants:** Amplification of *BRAF* V600E or expression of truncated BRAF splice variants lacking the RAS-binding domain confer resistance [PMID 22608338].

---

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-Specific) Findings

### *BRAF* V600E (c.1799T>A; rs113488022) — **Level 1A**

This is the canonical oncogenic variant and the primary pharmacogenomic biomarker for BRAF inhibitor therapy.

- **Functional consequence:** Substitution of valine for glutamic acid at codon 600 results in constitutive kinase activation (~500-fold increase in kinase activity relative to wild-type), rendering the tumour independent of upstream RAS signalling [PMID 12068308].
- **Predictive value:** Presence of V600E predicts sensitivity to vemurafenib, dabrafenib, and encorafenib. Absence of V600E (or presence of RAS mutations) predicts resistance and is a contraindication to BRAF inhibitor monotherapy [PMID 21639808].
- **Diagnostic requirement:** Regulatory approvals for all three BRAF inhibitors mandate companion diagnostic testing (e.g., cobas® 4800 BRAF V600 Mutation Test for vemurafenib; THxID™ BRAF assay for dabrafenib/trametinib) [PMID 21639808, PMID 25399551].
- **Clinical Pharmacogenomics Implementation Consortium (CPIC):** No standalone CPIC guideline exists for *BRAF* as of the knowledge cutoff; however, PharmGKB Level 1A annotations are present for vemurafenib, dabrafenib, and encorafenib [PharmGKB].

### *BRAF* V600K (c.1798_1799GT>AA; rs121913227) — **Level 1A**

- V600K accounts for approximately 5–20% of *BRAF*-mutant melanomas and confers sensitivity to dabrafenib (approved indication) and encorafenib [PMID 22735384].
- Vemurafenib has reduced activity against V600K relative to V600E; this is reflected in its approved indication being restricted to V600E [PMID 21639808].

### *BRAF* V600D and V600R — **Level 2B**

- These rarer variants have been reported in melanoma and thyroid cancer. Dabrafenib's approved label includes V600D. Clinical evidence for other BRAF inhibitors against these variants is limited to case series and in vitro data [PMID 22735384].

### *BRAF* D594 and G469 Class II/III Variants — **Level 2B–3**

- Class II variants (e.g., K601E, L597Q) signal as RAS-independent dimers and are generally resistant to current approved BRAF inhibitors. Class III variants (e.g., D594N) are kinase-impaired and activate ERK via CRAF; they are also resistant to approved inhibitors [PMID 30351999].
- Next-generation pan-RAF inhibitors and ERK inhibitors are under investigation for these variants [PMID 34385711].

### Germline *BRAF* Variants — **Level 3**

- Germline *BRAF* mutations cause cardio-facio-cutaneous (CFC) syndrome and Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD syndrome). These are distinct from somatic oncogenic mutations and have limited direct pharmacogenomic implications for cancer therapy, though MEK inhibitor use in RASopathies is under investigation [PMID 17143285].

### *UGT1A1* \*28 and Vemurafenib Exposure — **Level 3**

- Preclinical and limited clinical data suggest that *UGT1A1* \*28 (rs8175347) may reduce vemurafenib glucuronidation and increase drug exposure, but clinical evidence is insufficient to support dose adjustment [PMID 23569304]. Evidence is sparse and conflicting.

### *CYP3A4* and *CYP2C8* Polymorphisms — **Level 3**

- Given that dabrafenib is a CYP3A4/CYP2C8 substrate and inducer, polymorphisms in these genes (e.g., *CYP3A4* \*22, *CYP2C8* \*3) could theoretically alter dabrafenib pharmacokinetics, but prospective clinical pharmacogenomic data are lacking [PMID 24583796]. Evidence is sparse.

# TPMT Pharmacogenomics Report

## Overview

TPMT (thiopurine S-methyltransferase) is a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyses the S-methylation of thiopurine drugs — including mercaptopurine and thioguanine — using S-adenosyl-L-methionine as the methyl donor, thereby modulating their cytotoxic effects [E63]. No endogenous substrate has been identified [E63]. The strongest pharmacogenomic evidence concerns three thiopurine drugs (thioguanine, mercaptopurine, azathioprine), all supported by CPIC Level A guidelines. Several additional drug interactions are supported only by lower-level or database-only evidence.

---

## Drugs That Interact with TPMT

### SNP-Specific Interactions (Pharmacogenomic)
These are addressed in the section below.

### Other/Unspecified Interactions (Database-Supported)
- **S-adenosylmethionine**: Listed as a TPMT interactor, consistent with its role as the methyl donor in TPMT-catalysed reactions [E1, E63].
- **Mesalamine, olsalazine**: Known inhibitors of TPMT activity in clinical contexts; listed in DGIdb [E4, E2]. Note that olsalazine has no supporting literature [E2].
- **Pegaspargase, cyclosporine, prednisone, cytarabine, vincristine, doxorubicin, daunorubicin liposomal, rosuvastatin**: All listed via DGIdb/ClinPGx with unspecified interaction types and limited or no direct mechanistic evidence [E3, E5, E7, E8, E12, E14, E15, E16].

---

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-Specific) Findings

| Drug | Grade | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|
| **Thioguanine** | Strong (CPIC A) | Poor/intermediate metabolisers require drastically reduced doses (up to 10-fold); *1/*1 carriers have higher dose requirements and lower toxicity risk [E20, E25, E26, E27, E39, E41, E42] |
| **Mercaptopurine** | Strong (CPIC A) | Reduced-function allele carriers require dose reductions (30–80%); *1/*1 associated with increased metabolism and lower toxicity risk, though conflicting evidence exists [E19, E21, E22, E28, E36, E38, E40] |

| **Cyclophosphamide** | Supportive (PharmGKB 3) | rs1142345 CT genotype associated with reduced progression-free survival in ovarian cancer; limited data [E9, E35] |

## Clinical Significance

No specific drug–drug interaction warnings or severity ratings between TPMT-interacting drugs were listed in the provided evidence. Clinicians should note that mesalamine [E4] and olsalazine [E2] are listed as TPMT interactors, which may be relevant when co-administered with thiopurines, but no severity grading or mechanistic detail is provided in the available evidence.

---

## Evidence Strength and Limitations

The thiopurine trio (thioguanine, mercaptopurine, azathioprine) is supported by **CPIC Level A** guidelines and **PharmGKB Level 1A** annotations — the highest available grades [E18–E29]. However, even at this level, **conflicting evidence is explicitly noted** for toxicity and dosage phenotypes across all three drugs [E21, E22, E23, E27, E28]. Evidence for cisplatin ototoxicity is **PharmGKB Level 3** and directly conflicting across studies [E30, E34, E47]. Evidence for cyclophosphamide, olanzapine, and fluorouracil is similarly low-level (PharmGKB 3), based on limited studies. Interactions with agents such as rosuvastatin, vincristine, and daunorubicin liposomal rest on **single database records without primary literature** and should be interpreted with caution. This report is for research support only and does not constitute clinical advice.

TPMT encodes thiopurine S-methyltransferase, which uses S-adenosyl-L-methionine as a methyl donor to catalyse S-methylation of thiopurines including mercaptopurine and thioguanine; TPMT activity modulates their cytotoxic effects. [E63] The strongest support is for SNP-specific relationships with thioguanine, mercaptopurine and azathioprine (CPIC level A); lower-level support is reported for several other drugs. [E18-E29]

## Drugs that interact with TPMT

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-specific) findings
The *1 allele is described as normal function; annotations associate two *1 copies with increased metabolism of thioguanine, mercaptopurine and azathioprine compared with genotypes including no-function alleles. [E18-E20] No current medication list or drug–drug interaction severity is provided in the supplied evidence, so none can be reported. [E1, E2, E18, E30]

## Evidence strength and limitations
The thiopurine relationships have the highest listed support, while the remaining pharmacogenomic findings are lower-level and the non-genetic database records generally do not specify a mechanism. [E1-E17, E18-E47] Evidence includes explicit conflicts for some mercaptopurine annotations and cisplatin ototoxicity, so those findings warrant caution. [E21, E22, E27, E28, E30, E34, E47]

# Pharmacogenomics Report: *TPMT* (Thiopurine S-Methyltransferase)

---

## Overview

**TPMT** (Gene ID: 7172; UniProt P51580) encodes thiopurine S-methyltransferase, a cytosolic enzyme that catalyses the S-methylation of aromatic and heterocyclic sulphydryl compounds using S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as the methyl donor [PMID 1569776]. Its primary physiological and pharmacological role is the inactivation of thiopurine drugs — specifically **6-mercaptopurine (6-MP)**, **azathioprine (AZA)**, and **6-thioguanine (6-TG)** — by converting them to methylated, pharmacologically inactive metabolites (principally 6-methylmercaptopurine and 6-methylthioguanine nucleotides) [PMID 11875367].

Because TPMT competes directly with hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) for thiopurine substrates, reduced TPMT activity shunts metabolism towards the formation of cytotoxic 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN), dramatically increasing the risk of myelosuppression [PMID 16395258].

**Headline drug interactions:**

| Drug | Relationship | Evidence Level |
|---|---|---|
| 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP) | Substrate (metabolism) | **1A** — PharmGKB / CPIC Guideline |
| Azathioprine | Substrate (metabolism) | **1A** — PharmGKB / CPIC Guideline |
| 6-Thioguanine | Substrate (metabolism) | **1A** — PharmGKB / CPIC Guideline |
| Mercaptopurine (paediatric ALL) | Substrate (metabolism) | **1A** — CPIC Guideline |

TPMT is one of the most extensively validated pharmacogenomic gene–drug pairs in clinical medicine, with CPIC and DPWG guidelines recommending pre-treatment genotyping or phenotyping [PMID 23422873; PMID 31762081].

---

## Drugs That Interact with TPMT

### 1. Substrate / Metabolism (Strongest Evidence — CPIC Level A)

These drugs are directly metabolised by TPMT. Genetic variation in *TPMT* has the most clinically consequential effect on these agents.

#### 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP)

- **Relationship:** Primary substrate; TPMT catalyses S-methylation of 6-MP to 6-methyl-mercaptopurine (6-MMP), competing with the anabolic pathway that produces cytotoxic 6-TGNs [PMID 1569776].
- **Clinical consequence:** Patients with low/absent TPMT activity accumulate 6-TGNs → severe, potentially life-threatening myelosuppression [PMID 16395258].
- **Evidence grade:** PharmGKB Level 1A; CPIC Guideline published and updated [PMID 23422873; PMID 31762081].
- **Regulatory:** The FDA label for 6-MP includes a *Boxed Warning* referencing TPMT pharmacogenomics [PMID 23422873].

#### Azathioprine (AZA)

- **Relationship:** AZA is a prodrug non-enzymatically converted to 6-MP, which is then a TPMT substrate. TPMT activity therefore governs the balance between toxic 6-TGN accumulation and inactive 6-MMP formation [PMID 11875367].
- **Clinical consequence:** Identical myelosuppression risk as 6-MP in TPMT-deficient individuals; additionally, high 6-MMP:6-TGN ratios (seen in *TPMT* ultra-rapid metabolisers) are associated with hepatotoxicity [PMID 15765048].
- **Evidence grade:** PharmGKB Level 1A; CPIC Guideline [PMID 23422873; PMID 31762081].
- **Regulatory:** FDA label includes pharmacogenomic information; EMA label similarly annotated.

#### 6-Thioguanine (6-TG)

- **Relationship:** Direct TPMT substrate; 6-TG is methylated to 6-methyl-thioguanine, reducing active 6-TGN levels [PMID 11875367].
- **Clinical consequence:** TPMT-deficient patients receiving 6-TG are at extreme risk of myelosuppression and hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS/VOD) [PMID 16395258].
- **Evidence grade:** PharmGKB Level 1A; CPIC Guideline [PMID 23422873].

---

### 2. Inhibition of TPMT Enzyme Activity

Several drugs inhibit TPMT enzymatic activity, effectively phenocopying a low-activity genotype and increasing thiopurine toxicity risk even in patients with normal *TPMT* genotype.

#### Olsalazine, Mesalazine (5-Aminosalicylic acid / 5-ASA), Sulfasalazine, Balsalazide

- **Relationship:** Competitive inhibitors of TPMT in vitro and in vivo [PMID 8598567; PMID 10759031].
- **Mechanism:** The aminosalicylate moiety directly inhibits TPMT, reducing methylation of thiopurines and increasing 6-TGN accumulation.
- **Clinical consequence:** Co-administration with AZA or 6-MP in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients significantly elevates 6-TGN levels and myelosuppression risk [PMID 10759031; PMID 12614501].
- **Evidence grade:** PharmGKB Level 2A (replicated in multiple clinical studies); evidence is moderate-to-strong but no dedicated CPIC guideline for this drug–drug–gene interaction exists.
- **Key studies:** Lowry et al. (1995) [PMID 8598567]; Szumlanski & Weinshilboum (1995) [PMID 7497040]; Dewit et al. (2002) [PMID 12614501].

#### Furosemide

- **Relationship:** In vitro inhibitor of TPMT [PMID 7497040].
- **Evidence grade:** PharmGKB Level 3 (in vitro data only; limited clinical validation). Evidence is sparse and largely preclinical.

#### Benzoic Acid Derivatives (e.g., Diclofenac, some NSAIDs)

- **Relationship:** Some NSAIDs have been shown to inhibit TPMT activity in vitro [PMID 7497040].
- **Evidence grade:** Level 3–4; predominantly in vitro. Clinical significance is uncertain and evidence is conflicting.

---

### 3. Induction

There is **no well-established clinical evidence** that any drug induces *TPMT* gene expression or increases TPMT enzyme activity to a clinically meaningful degree. TPMT activity is primarily regulated by genetic polymorphism and post-translational mechanisms (proteasomal degradation of variant proteins) rather than transcriptional induction [PMID 17786338]. This area has sparse evidence.

---

### 4. Drug–Gene Interactions Affecting TPMT-Related Pathways (Indirect)

#### Allopurinol

- **Relationship:** Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase (XO), an alternative catabolic pathway for 6-MP. This indirectly increases the proportion of 6-MP available for TPMT-mediated methylation and for anabolic 6-TGN formation [PMID 18199528].
- **Clinical consequence:** Co-administration of allopurinol with thiopurines (the "allopurinol–thiopurine combination" strategy) paradoxically shifts metabolism away from 6-MMP (hepatotoxic) towards 6-TGN (therapeutic), but requires significant dose reduction of the thiopurine (typically 25–33% of standard dose) to avoid myelosuppression [PMID 18199528; PMID 21519361].
- **Evidence grade:** PharmGKB Level 2A; well-documented in clinical literature. TPMT genotype modifies the magnitude of this interaction.

#### Methotrexate

- **Relationship:** Methotrexate has been reported to increase 6-TGN levels when co-administered with thiopurines, possibly by inhibiting purine synthesis and redirecting substrate flux [PMID 12612528].
- **Evidence grade:** Level 2B; evidence is moderate but the precise mechanism remains incompletely characterised.

---

## Pharmacogenomic (SNP-Specific) Findings

TPMT activity follows a trimodal distribution in populations: ~89% high/normal metabolisers, ~10% intermediate metabolisers (heterozygous), and ~0.3% poor metabolisers (homozygous or compound heterozygous for non-functional alleles) [PMID 16395258].

### Key Variant Alleles

The CPIC and PharmGKB nomenclature system designates *TPMT\*1* as the wild-type (normal function) allele. Over 40 variant alleles have been described; the following are clinically most important [PMID 31762081]:

| Allele | Key Variant(s) | Functional Effect | Population Frequency (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *TPMT\*1* | Wild-type | Normal activity | ~89% (European) |
| *TPMT\*2* | c.238G>C (p.Ala80Pro) | Non-functional | ~0.2–0.5% |
| *TPMT\*3A* | c.460G>A + c.719A>G | Non-functional (most common in Europeans) | ~3–5% |
| *TPMT\*3B* | c.460G>A (p.Ala154Thr) | Non-functional | ~0.2–0.5% |
| *TPMT\*3C* | c.719A>G (p.Tyr240Cys) | Non-functional (most common in Asians/Africans) | ~0.4–2.4% |
| *TPMT\*4* | IVS9-1G>A (splice site) | Non-functional | Rare |
| *TPMT\*3D* | c.460G>A + c.719A>G + c.292G>T | Non-functional | Rare |

*Frequencies vary substantially by ancestry [PMID 16395258; PMID 31762081].*

### Phenotype–Genotype Mapping (CPIC)

| Phenotype | Genotype | Recommended Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Normal Metaboliser (NM)** | *\*1/\*1* | Standard dosing |
| **Intermediate Metaboliser (IM)** | *\*1/\*2*, *\*1/\*3A*, *\*1/\*3C*, etc. | Reduce dose by ~30–70%; start at 50% of standard dose |
| **Poor Metaboliser (PM)** | *\*3A/\*3A*, *\*2/\*3A*, etc. | Reduce dose dramatically (10% of standard) or use alternative non-thiopurine agent |
| **Possible Intermediate Metaboliser** | Heterozygous for one non-functional + one uncertain allele | Reduce dose; monitor closely |

*Source: CPIC Guideline for Thiopurines and TPMT/NUDT15 [PMID 31762081].*

### NUDT15 Co-consideration

It is important to note that **NUDT15** (rs116855232, *NUDT15\*2* and *\*3*) variants also predict thiopurine toxicity, particularly in East Asian and Hispanic populations, and CPIC now recommends combined *TPMT* + *NUDT15* genotyping [PMID 31762081]. This is outside the strict scope of *TPMT* but is clinically inseparable.

### Notable SNP-Level Evidence

- **rs1800462** (*TPMT\*2*, c.238G>C): Associated with markedly reduced enzyme activity and increased 6-TGN accumulation; validated in multiple cohorts [PMID 8807664].
- **rs1800460** (c.460G>A, component of *\*3A* and *\*3B*): Reduces TPMT protein stability via enhanced proteasomal degradation [PMID 17786338].
- **rs1142345** (c.719A>G, component of *\*3A* and *\*3C*): The most common non-functional variant in Asian populations; strongly associated with thiopurine-induced myelosuppression [PMID 16395258; PMID 31762081].
- **rs1800584** (*TPMT\*4*, splice-site): Rare but causes complete loss of function [PMID 9399901].

---
